newsitem.title: UK: Strong dollar key to EMU policy log-jam - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Strong dollar key to EMU policy log-jam - analysts.

text.p: Governments of the industrialised world will do whatever necessary to keep the dollar strong to counteract the impact on world growth of severe fiscal tightening ahead of European monetary union, economists said.

There is a growing feeling that the global policy concern about the EMU squeeze has fostered agreed contingency plans within leading economic forums such as the Group of Seven rich industrial nations.

Any agreement to offset the fiscal shellshock around EMU would need to effectively underwrite relatively loose European monetary policy and a stronger dollar over the next two or three years, analysts said.
This scenario has been crucial in fuelling the overwhelming desire for yield convergence trades of late, say analysts.

The fact the authorities have a vested interest in maintaining this global environment means the attraction of yield convergence is not simply isolated to countries likely to start EMU. UK markets are a case in point.
"Plan "A' for the bulk of the G7 is that a higher dollar will break the policy log-jam it is facing," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank.

Analysts point to the apparent turnaround in U.S. policy over the past two years -- from benign neglect in the early part of the Clinton presidency to the current mantra of calling for a strong dollar.
European countries, most vociferously France, have been more vocal for longer.

French finance minister Jean Arthuis said last month that the European Commission estimates the exchange rate between the dollar and the European currency unit over recent years has cost Europe more than one percentage point in growth.
Against this backdrop the planned EMU-related fiscal retrenchment is not in any way consistent with a weak dollar.

The breakneck scramble in nearly all European Union countries to meet the budgetary and debt entry criteria for monetary union will suck billions of dollars of public money out of economies already experiencing sub-par economic actrivity.
The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, the Paris-based 25-nation economic think-tank, warned in June about the impact fiscal tightening around EMU.

A simultaneous 1997 fiscal squeeze, even if limited to the EMU core countries, poses "the risk of a further weakening in aggregate demand -- or even perhaps recession -- in the short run," the OECD said.
"I think everyone now realises that with the impact on growth of EMU budgets, Europe just simply can't afford to raise interest rates," said Henry Wilkes, trader at Bank Julius Baer.

The impact on European domestic demand of the fiscal tightening means Europe needs to export its way through the next few years. That means it cannot afford to allow either a falling dollar to usurp its competitiveness or a slowing U.S. economy to dry up its key export markets.

The problem, however, is that sub-par growth in Europe relative the U.S. for years now has already ballooned Europe's trade surplus with the U.S.. The bilateral trade gap soared 457.8 percent in July to its highest ever recorded level.

Because the trade imbalance alone is a big negative for the dollar, the price of U.S. currency can only remain supported if the gap in supply in demand for dollars is met either by private portfolio flows to relatively higher U.S. yields or by official central bank purchases of dollars.
In is no accident, analysts argue, that European central bank holdings of dollars have been rising steeply again over the past two years.

"A key fuel to EMU optimism is the current low interest rate environment and low and falling interest rates in Germany and other portfolio exporters such as the U.S. and Japan," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency researcxh at JP Morgan.

"What the authorities know is that if world interest rates remain low, you can expect EMU optimism to remain high and the dollar to rally against the mark even without a higher U.S. rate differential," said Persaud at JP Morgan.
